latest_final: The narrator deliberately murdered their own spouse. To conceal the murder, the narrator needed it to look as though the spouse had not been killed but had instead walked out and left the narrator for good—so the narrator set out to forge a farewell note in the dead spouse's handwriting. The repeated identical line, "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back," is the text of that fake abandonment note, and the many copies are the narrator's practice drafts: the narrator handwrote the same sentence over and over to rehearse/imitate the dead spouse's handwriting well enough that the forged "I'm leaving you and never coming back" note would pass as genuinely written by the victim. It is one hand writing repeatedly (not several speakers, not a machine or recording, not a printed book), and this is why the line is both "addressed to the narrator" (it is a message from the spouse to the narrator) and not (the narrator is only fabricating it). Looking at the failed practice copies, the narrator sighs, "I know I'm in trouble"—realizing these incriminating forgeries will expose the murder and the lie that the spouse simply left.
